note: Start with a moderate C5/C6 split to create two manageable, valuable cuts and measure purity and cost.
notebook:

Root first: 60 stages, R=B=3.5, 10% pressure drop. Target lights through N-pentane overhead and C6+ bottoms. This keeps initial exploration simple while revealing achievable split and annual cost.

note: Build four blend-producing cuts: split C4 from C5, C3 from C4, and C6 paraffins from heavier material.
notebook:
PLAN: Step 1 establish a sharp C5/C6 feed split and inspect costs/purities. Step 2 branch both cuts into high-value pure products/blends, using moderate stages/reflux. Step 3 prune low-value separations and tune expensive columns; consider side draws/double effect only if economics justify.
Root at 60/3.5/3.5/.1 gives a useful C5/C6 split and costs $221M/yr. Now add T: C4/C5 split, TT: C3/C4 split, and B: C6-paraffins/heavies split. Goal is immediate sale of C3, C4, C5 and C6-paraffin blends; inspect leakage before adding harder pure-product columns. Other agent confirms coarse 45-stage branches alone do not reach specs.

note: Sharpen all four cuts enough to sell the four light/middle blends; this establishes revenue before economic tuning.
notebook:
PLAN: Step 1 establish a sharp C5/C6 feed split and inspect costs/purities. Step 2 branch both cuts into high-value pure products/blends, using moderate stages/reflux. Step 3 prune low-value separations and tune expensive columns; consider side draws/double effect only if economics justify.
The coarse cascade failed because every blend was badly contaminated. Sharpen root (C5/C6), T (C4/C5), TT (C3/C4), and B (C6 paraffins/heavies) together to obtain the first revenue. Target C3, C4, C5, and C6-paraffin blends. Costs are high, so after achieving sales I will reduce stages/reflux and drop marginal branches.

note: Restructure into three direct blend cuts: C4/C5 at the root, C3/C4 above, and C5/C6 below. This should avoid the severe contamination of the previous cascade.
notebook:
PLAN: Step 1 restructure to a direct C4/C5 root split, then C3/C4 and C5/C6 branch cuts. Step 2 establish revenue from C3/C4/C5 blends. Step 3 add C6-paraffin recovery only if profitable and tune stages/reflux aggressively.
The old C5/C6-first cascade wastes a huge root column and contaminates every branch. A C4/C5 root uses the much wider N-butane/isopentane volatility gap. The T branch now directly makes C3 and C4 blends; B separates the valuable C5 blend from C6+. I removed the redundant TT column. Root/T use moderate severity; B gets high severity for the closer C5/C6 cut.

note: Push all three group splits into the sharp-cut regime at an intermediate pressure, avoiding the failed extreme root while improving volatility.
notebook:
PLAN: Step 1 restructure to a direct C4/C5 root split, then C3/C4 and C5/C6 branch cuts. Step 2 establish revenue from C3/C4/C5 blends. Step 3 add C6-paraffin recovery only if profitable and tune stages/reflux aggressively.
The current cuts remain far too sloppy: the root sends ~350 mol/s C5 overhead and both branches retain large amounts of the adjacent group. Agent-9 shows that 100/8/8 at 0.1 is still inadequate and very costly, while 140/12 at 0.5 fails. I am testing an intermediate robust operating point: higher reflux/boil-up than before, 0.3 pressure drop to improve relative volatility, and fewer stages than the failed case. First obtain any qualifying blends, then reduce severity and remove low-value separations.

note: Remove the loss-making light-end column and retain only the proven C6-paraffin revenue, while sharply reducing the cost of both required cuts.
notebook:
PLAN: Focus on the most profitable simple plant: two columns making the C6-paraffin blend, with the C5-and-lighter tops sold as-is (worth zero). First establish a positive reward at moderate severity, then tune the two cuts and only add a C5 recovery branch if its revenue clearly exceeds its cost.
The current root is actually a good C5/C6 split and B already sells $1121M/yr of C6 paraffins; T is an expensive failed C3/C4/C5 separation. High severity is uneconomic: root+B cost $1218M/yr. Removing T immediately saves $267M/yr. Test 60 stages and reflux/boil-up 6 at 0.2 pressure drop on both columns; the wide nC5/C6 and nC6/methylcyclopentane gaps should retain blend purity at much lower cost.

note: Restore the proven C6 blend cut while lowering pressure and slightly relaxing the easy root split to reduce utility and refrigeration costs.
notebook:
PLAN: Focus on the two-column C6-paraffin plant. Restore proven blend purity, then reduce pressure and severity to find a positive-cost operating point before considering other products.
At 60/6 both cuts were too sloppy. The shown 90/12, dp0.3 plant reliably sells $1121M/yr of C6 paraffins, but costs $1218M/yr for root+B. The root split is wide (nC5/2,2-DMB), so it should tolerate reflux 10. Testing both columns at dp0.4 should lower condenser/reboiler temperatures and duties; B retains 90/12 because nC6/MCP is the harder split. Unsold light tops and heavy bottoms are acceptable for now.

note: The current C6 blend is far above its 95% specification, so aggressively reduce stages and reflux while retaining enough separation for saleable purity.
notebook:
PLAN: Focus on the two-column C6-paraffin plant. Restore proven blend purity, then reduce pressure and severity to find a positive-cost operating point before considering other products.
At 60/6 both cuts were too sloppy. The 90/10-12, dp0.4 plant sells $1132.6M/yr but costs $1185.5M/yr, nearly breakeven. BT is 99+% C6, so substantial slack exists against the 95% blend specification. Test a much cheaper root (50/5, dp0.5) and B (70/8, dp0.4): root only needs to keep most C5 out of B, while B needs <5% total light/heavy contamination. Unsold light tops and heavy bottoms are acceptable for now.

note: Interpolate between the cheap impure plant and R78's profitable operating point, targeting the root's N-pentane leakage and a modest reduction in B severity.
notebook:

Step: interpolate between my cheap but impure 50/5 + 70/8 design and R78's profitable 70/9 + 70/10 design. Test root 60/7 dp0.4 and B 70/9 dp0.4. The root mainly controls N-pentane contamination; B controls C6 vs heavier naphthenes. If this sells, relax whichever column has purity slack. R78 gives revenue $1114.9M and reward 0.172; my current cheap plant has 92% C6 due chiefly to 6% N-pentane, so most gain must come from the root. Avoid light-end train: prior attempts very costly and no sales.

note: Use R78's profitable backbone but exploit the better separation seen at lower pressure; test dp 0.3 on both columns and relax the second cut slightly.
notebook:

Step: start from R78's profitable 70/9 + 70/10 dp0.4 design and lower both pressures to dp0.3, also relaxing B to 9/9. R68 showed dp0.3 gives excellent C6 purity, so this may retain sales while cutting utility/capital cost. R78 baseline: revenue $1114.9M, cost $1039.4M, reward 0.172. My 60/7 root leaves 6% N-pentane and only 93% C6, so root severity is critical. Avoid the light-end train: it has repeatedly been costly and marginal.

note: Restore R97's profitable backbone and reduce both stages and reflux in its C6 column, whose product remains comfortably above blend specification.
notebook:

Step: restore R97 exactly (root 70/9/9/dp0.4, B 60/9/9/dp0.4), then test B at 50/8/8/dp0.4. R97 earns $1107.2M with $995.6M cost and reward 0.254; its C6 stream is about 98% blend, leaving room to reduce B severity. My dp0.3 experiment failed at the root (92% C6), confirming that root pressure and pentane leakage control feasibility. Avoid the light-end train: prior versions were costly and marginal.

note: Add R87's inexpensive one-sided C5 stripper to the now-proven severe root. Its revenue should be much higher here because the root sends nearly all C5 into T.
notebook: PLAN: First test a cheap one-sided C5 recovery column on the proven severe-root/C6 backbone; if profitable, tune it, then resume relaxing the C6 cut. Step: add T at R87's 90/2/10/dp0.4. Current best reward 0.332: root 70/9/9/dp0.4 and B 50/8/8/dp0.4; C6 blend is near its 95% limit, so further B relaxation is risky. R87's one-sided T column cost only $129M and sold $304M despite a weaker root; current T contains about 676 mol/s C5, potentially ~$600M revenue. Do not relax root pressure: dp0.3 caused C6 failure via pentane leakage.

note: Reduce stripper stages and boil-up to recover more of its abundant C5 while cutting cost; purity has ample margin.
notebook: PLAN: Optimize the profitable C5 stripper for recovery and cost, then relax the C6 column if margin allows. Step: test T at 70/2/7/dp0.4. T bottoms are 100% C5 but recover only 351 of about 676 mol/s C5; lowering boil-up should increase bottoms recovery and reduce duty, with C6 leakage as the risk. Root/B are near purity limits; do not lower root dp. TT and BB remain unsold and are not worth another costly train yet.

note: Continue the successful C5-stripper trend: fewer stages and less boil-up should recover more C5 at lower cost while retaining blend purity.
notebook: PLAN: Optimize the profitable C5 stripper for recovery and cost, then relax the C6 column if margin allows. Step: test T at 60/2/5/dp0.4. TT and BB remain unsold and are not worth another costly train yet.

Root 70/9/9 costs $590.5M and B 50/8/8 costs $361.5M; broad cuts to 8/8 and 7.5/7.5 were poor, so avoid repeating them. TT and BB remain unsold.

Preserve best; TT and BB otherwise unsold.

Next consider a modest TT trim only if C4 purity margin remains adequate.

notebook: PLAN: Preserve the four-column product backbone and use remaining solves to activate the large C6 heat-link saving without losing its blend.
